sections.skill: Tell written rules from learned patterns

questions.domain: Foundation 1: What AI is and where it appears
questions.prompt: A checkout page gives free shipping whenever an order is over 50 dollars. How was this behavior most likely produced?

choices.text: It learned from many past orders
It copied what a chatbot suggested
A person wrote a rule for it
It guessed the amount at random

questions.correct_answer: A person wrote a rule for it
questions.intro: Some software follows RULES that a person wrote: "If the total is over 50 dollars, apply free shipping." Every step was decided in advance, so you can read the rule to see why the program acted. Other systems LEARN PATTERNS from examples. A spam filter shown thousands of emails marked "spam" or "not spam" adjusts itself until it sorts new emails well. No one wrote a rule for every case; its behavior comes from the examples it learned from. Rule-based software is predictable but cannot handle cases its rules miss. Learned systems handle messy, varied input but can make surprising mistakes.
questions.feedback: A fixed "if over 50, then free" step is a written rule.

sections.skill: Compare a recipe with learning by tasting

questions.domain: Foundation 1: What AI is and where it appears
questions.prompt: Which cook is like rule-based software?

choices.text: The one who follows the recipe exactly
The one who learned by tasting many soups
The one who refuses to cook new dishes
The one who changes the recipe at random

questions.correct_answer: The one who follows the recipe exactly
questions.intro: Imagine two cooks. The first follows a RECIPE exactly: "Add 2 teaspoons of salt." If the recipe is right, the soup is right, and if anyone asks why, the cook points to the recipe. The second cook LEARNED BY TASTING hundreds of soups and adjusting until they tasted good. She can handle new ingredients the recipe never mentions, but she cannot always explain exactly why she added what she did, and sometimes she gets a new dish wrong. Rule-based software is like the recipe cook. Systems that learn patterns from examples are like the tasting cook.
questions.feedback: A recipe is a set of written rules.

sections.title: Apply it

sections.skill: Find which part failed in a system that mixes rules and learning

questions.domain: Foundation 1: What AI is and where it appears
questions.prompt: A bank's model flags a normal grocery purchase as unusual, and a written rule then holds the payment. Which part made the first mistake?

choices.text: The grocery store's card reader
The learned model that flagged the purchase
The written rule that held the payment
The customer who bought the groceries

questions.correct_answer: The learned model that flagged the purchase
questions.intro: Many real products mix both approaches. A learned model might flag a bank transaction as unusual, and then a written rule decides what happens next, such as "hold any flagged payment over 1,000 dollars." When something goes wrong, the fix depends on which part failed. A wrong written rule can be found and rewritten. A learned pattern usually changes only by retraining with better or more examples, and its mistakes can be harder to explain. Rules give predictability where it matters most; learning helps with variety that rules cannot list in advance.
questions.feedback: The error began with the learned flag; the rule only followed it.
